{{short description|Refers to perceived or actual relationships between crime and immigration}}
{{Distinguish|Race and crime}}
{{use dmy dates|date=September 2023}}
{{Criminology and penology  |expanded=types}}
{{Immigration sidebar}}
The relationship between [[immigration]] and [[crime]] has been a subject of extensive research, political discourse, and public debate.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Marie |first1=Olivier |last2=Pinotti |first2=Paolo |date=March 2024 |title=Immigration and Crime: An International Perspective |url=https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jep.38.1.181 |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |language=en |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=181–200 |doi=10.1257/jep.38.1.181  |doi-access=free|issn=0895-3309}}</ref>

Immigrants are disproportionately represented in prison populations in many Western countries, though notable exceptions exist, [[Illegal immigration to the United States and crime|such as the United States]].<ref name=":70" /><ref name="z746">{{cite journal | last1=Cohn | first1=Ellen G. | last2=Coccia | first2=Mario | last3=Kakar | first3=Suman | title=Disparate incarceration rates of foreign citizens in Europe compared to Anglo-Saxon countries | journal=Sociology Compass | volume=18 | issue=1 | date=2024 | issn=1751-9020 | doi=10.1111/soc4.13167 | article-number=e13167 | quote=The principal findings suggest, in most European countries, a significantly higher rate of foreign citizens held in prison compared to non‐immigrants.}}</ref> In Europe and other regions, higher representation in prisons among immigrants, particularly Muslim populations, has been documented.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-09-09 |title=Let me take a wild guess as to why Muslims are overrepresented in prison |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/voices/lammy-review-prisons-bame-islamophobia-rehabilitation-discrimination-a7937746.html |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=The Independent |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Are 70% of France's prison inmates Muslims? |url=https://www.adamsmith.org/blog/are-70-of-frances-prison-inmates-muslims |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=Adam Smith Institute |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kern |first=Soeren |title=Germany: Number of Foreign-Born Prison Inmates at Record High |url=https://kern.pundicity.com/22364/germany-immigrants-prisons |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=Soeren Kern |language=en}}</ref> However, some of the factors contributing to these trends include imprisonment for migration-related offenses<ref>{{cite journal |last1=E. Martínez, Ph.D |first1=Daniel |last2=G. Rumbaut, Ph.D |first2=Rubén |title=The Criminalization of Immigration in the United States |journal=America Immigration Council |date=July 13, 2015 |url=https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/research/criminalization-immigration-united-states |access-date=23 December 2024}}</ref> and systemic bias in policing and judicial processes, which may inflate crime statistics for immigrant populations relative to their real criminal rate.<ref name=":27">{{Cite book |last=Crocitti |first=Stefania |title=Immigration, Crime, and Criminalization in Italy – Oxford Handbooks |year=2014 |doi=10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199859016.013.029}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=West |first=Jeremy |date=February 2018 |title=Racial Bias in Police Investigations |url=https://people.ucsc.edu/~jwest1/articles/West_RacialBiasPolice.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Working Paper |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190323090110/https://people.ucsc.edu/~jwest1/articles/West_RacialBiasPolice.pdf |archive-date=23 March 2019 |access-date=16 March 2018}}</ref> Research suggests that public perception often exaggerates the connection between '''immigration and crime''', influenced by sensationalised media coverage and political rhetoric. This can result in stricter immigration controls, as well as harsher immigration policies like [[family separation]]; along with a potential increase in [[hate crime]]s against immigrant communities.<ref name=":410">{{Cite web |last=Ajzenman |first=Nicolas |date=2023-01-29 |title=Migrants don't cause crime rates to increase — but false perceptions endure anyway |url=http://theconversation.com/migrants-dont-cause-crime-rates-to-increase-but-false-perceptions-endure-anyway-198054 |access-date=2024-08-05 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US |quote=Although most research shows immigration has either no impact or a minimal impact on crime, many people seem to believe the connection exists. It seems hostility against immigrants isn't crime itself but false perceptions about crime.}}</ref>

== Factors ==
Research relating to immigration and crime has been described as generally showing mixed results.<ref name="s183">{{cite journal |last1=Lange |first1=Martin |last2=Sommerfeld |first2=Katrin |year=2024 |title=Do refugees impact crime? Causal evidence from large-scale refugee immigration to Germany |journal=Labour Economics |publisher=Elsevier BV |volume=86 |article-number=102466 |doi=10.1016/j.labeco.2023.102466 |issn=0927-5371 |quote=Previous studies about the effect of immigration on crime show mixed results. Part of the literature finds the effects of immigration on crime in host countries to be close to zero in general ... Other studies tend to conclude that immigration increases crime under certain circumstances, particularly if immigrants have poor prospects on the labor market or if they face labor market restrictions.|hdl=10419/297106 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

While immigrants are overrepresented in prison populations in many Western countries, with notable exceptions such as the United States, some studies<ref name=":70" /> fail to show a causal effect of immigration on overall crime rates.{{Refn|<ref name=":70">{{Cite journal |last1=Marie |first1=Olivier |last2=Pinotti |first2=Paolo |date=2024-02-01 |title=Immigration and Crime: An International Perspective |url=https://pubs.aeaweb.org/doi/10.1257/jep.38.1.181 |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |language=en |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=181–200 |doi=10.1257/jep.38.1.181  |doi-access=free|issn=0895-3309 |quote=On one side, in most countries—with the notable exception of the United States—immigrants exhibit a disproportionate involvement in criminal activity compared to natives, as measured by the relative incarceration rate of the two groups. In addition, certain kinds of immigrants, including young and less-educated men and those with irregular legal status, display a much higher propensity to commit crimes than those with documented status. These factors would seem to suggest a positive link between immigration and crime. On the other side, studies designed to measure the effect of immigration inflow effects on local crime rates do not, in general, find any detectable causal effect of immigration on local crime rates. For example, all previous studies relying on the shift-share instrumental variable approach estimate crime elasticities close to zero in various countries, and we further confirm this result on new data across European countries and regions.}}</ref><ref name=":71">{{Cite journal |last1=Tufail |first1=Muhammad |last2=Song |first2=Lin |last3=Ali |first3=Sher |last4=Wahab |first4=Salman |last5=Hassan |first5=Taimoor |date=2023-03-31 |title=Does more immigration lead to more violent and property crimes? A case study of 30 selected OECD countries |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1331677X.2022.2094437 |journal=[[Economic Research-Ekonomska Istraživanja]] |language=en |volume=36 Some factors may affect the reliability of data on suspect rates, crime rates, conviction rates and prison populations for drawing conclusions about immigrants' overall involvement in criminal activity:
* Police practices, such as [[racial profiling]], over-policing in areas populated by immigrants or in-group bias may result in disproportionately high numbers of immigrants among crime suspects.<ref name=":27"/><ref name=":12">{{Cite journal|title = Crime as a Price of Inequality? The Gap in Registered Crime between Childhood Immigrants, Children of Immigrants and Children of Native Swedes |journal = British Journal of Criminology|date = 2013-05-01|issn = 0007-0955|pages = 456–481|volume = 53|issue = 3|doi = 10.1093/bjc/azt005|first1 = Martin|last1 = Hällsten|first2 = Ryszard|last2 = Szulkin|first3 = Jerzy|last3 = Sarnecki}}</ref><ref name="ItalyPenal">{{Cite journal|last=Colombo|first=Asher|date=2013-11-01|title=Foreigners and immigrants in Italy's penal and administrative detention systems |journal=European Journal of Criminology |language=en |volume=10 |issue=6 |pages=746–759 |doi=10.1177/1477370813495128|s2cid=145099179|issn=1477-3708}}</ref><ref name=":23" /><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Racial profiling and searches: Did the politics of racial profiling change police behavior?* |journal = Criminology & Public Policy|date = 2009-05-01|issn = 1745-9133|pages = 343–369|volume = 8|issue = 2|doi = 10.1111/j.1745-9133.2009.00556.x|language = en|first1 = Patricia Y.|last1 = Warren|first2 = Donald|last2 = Tomaskovic-Devey}}</ref>
* Possible discrimination by the judicial system may result in higher number of convictions.<ref name=":27" /><ref name="ItalyPenal" /><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Do Judges Vary in Their Treatment of Race?|journal = The Journal of Legal Studies|date = 2012-06-01|issn = 0047-2530|pages = 347–383|volume = 41|issue = 2|doi = 10.1086/666006|first1 = David S.|last1 = Abrams|first2 = Marianne|last2 = Bertrand|first3 = Sendhil|last3 = Mullainathan|s2cid = 2338687|url = https://scholarship.law.upenn.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1354&context=faculty_scholarship|access-date = 18 August 2019|archive-date = 13 November 2019|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20191113123439/http://scholarship.law.upenn.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1354&context=faculty_scholarship|url-status = live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Racial, Ethnic, and Gender Disparities in Sentencing: Evidence from the U.S. Federal Courts |journal = The Journal of Law and Economics|date = 2001-04-01|issn = 0022-2186|pages = 285–314|volume = 44|issue = 1|doi = 10.1086/320276|first = David B.|last = Mustard|s2cid = 154533225}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title = The Impact of Jury Race in Criminal Trials |journal = The Quarterly Journal of Economics|date = 2012-05-01|issn = 0033-5533|pages = 1017–1055|volume = 127|issue = 2|doi = 10.1093/qje/qjs014|language = en|first1 = Shamena|last1 = Anwar|first2 = Patrick|last2 = Bayer|first3 = Randi|last3 = Hjalmarsson|doi-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Effects of Defendant Ethnicity on Juries' Dispositions of Felony Cases |journal = Journal of Applied Social Psychology|date = 1999-02-01|issn = 1559-1816|pages = 317–336|volume = 29|issue = 2|doi = 10.1111/j.1559-1816.1999.tb01389.x|language = en|first1 = Howard C.|last1 = Daudistel|first2 = Harmon M.|last2 = Hosch|first3 = Malcolm D.|last3 = Holmes|first4 = Joseph B.|last4 = Graves}}</ref>
* Unfavorable bail and sentencing decisions due to foreigners' ease of flight, lack of domiciles, lack of regular employment and lack of family able to host the individual can explain immigrants' higher incarceration rates when compared to their share of convictions relative to the native population.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":22" />
* Non-immigrants may be more likely to report crimes when they believe the offender has an [[Migration background|immigrant background]].<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.sociology.su.se/polopoly_fs/1.18650.1320939631!/rapport.pdf|title = Diskrimineras invandrarna i anmälningar av brott?|date = 2009|last = Dahlbäck|first = Olof|access-date = 31 January 2016|archive-date = 31 January 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160131153955/http://www.sociology.su.se/polopoly_fs/1.18650.1320939631!/rapport.pdf|url-status = live}}</ref>
* Imprisonment for migration offenses, which are more common among immigrants without a residence permit in their host country, would need to be excluded from the analysis of crime statistics for meaningful comparisons between overall immigrant and native criminal involvement.<ref name="ItalyPenal" /><ref name=":26">{{Cite web |date=2015 |title=Indvandrere i Danmark |trans-title=Immigrants in Denmark |url=http://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/Udgivelser/GetPubFile.aspx?id=20703&sid=indv2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160215235233/http://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/Udgivelser/GetPubFile.aspx?id=20703&sid=indv2015 |archive-date=15 February 2016 |access-date=10 February 2016 |publisher=Statistics Denmark |language=da}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Aliverti|first=Ana|url=https://www.routledge.com/products/9780415820905|title=Crimes of Mobility: Criminal Law and the Regulation of Immigration|year=2013|edition=hardback|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-415-82090-5|access-date=2016-03-04|archive-date=11 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160311191830/https://www.routledge.com/products/9780415820905|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{citation |mode=cs1|last=Bosworth|first=Mary|date=2011-05-01|title=Deportation, Detention and Foreign National Prisoners in England and Wales|ssrn=1852191|location=Rochester, NY|publisher=Social Science Research Network|doi=10.2139/ssrn.1852191}}</ref>
* Foreigners imprisoned for drug offenses may not actually live in the country where they are serving sentences but were arrested while in transit.<ref name=":26" />
*Crimes by short-term migrants, such as tourists, exchange students and transient workers, are in some cases counted as crimes by immigrants or foreigners, and gives the impression that a higher share of the migrant population commits crimes (as these short-term migrants are not counted among the foreign-born population).<ref>{{Citation|last1=Feltes|first1=Thomas|chapter=More Refugees, More Offenders, More Crime? Critical Comments with Data from Germany|date=2018|title=Refugees and Migrants in Law and Policy|pages=599–624|publisher=Springer International Publishing|language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-72159-0_26|isbn=978-3-319-72158-3|last2=List|first2=Katrin|last3=Bertamini|first3=Maximilian}}</ref>
*Some immigrants might disproportionately locate in deprived areas where crime is higher (because they cannot afford to stay in more expensive areas) or because they tend to locate in areas where there is a large population of residents of the same [[Migration background|ethnic background]].<ref name=":8" /> Some research suggests that the allocation of refugee immigrants to high crime neighborhoods increases individual crime propensity later in life due to social interaction with criminals.<ref name=":31">{{Cite journal |last1=Damm |first1=Anna Piil |last2=Dustmann |first2=Christian |year=2014 |title=Does Growing Up in a High Crime Neighborhood Affect Youth Criminal Behavior? |url=http://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/10038985/ |url-status=live |journal=[[American Economic Review]] |volume=104 |issue=6 |pages=1806–1832 |doi=10.1257/aer.104.6.1806 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210224235641/https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10038985/ |archive-date=24 February 2021 |access-date=18 August 2019 |via=[[UCL Discovery]]}}</ref>
*Granting legal status to undocumented immigrants might reduce crime rates among that population due to factors like greater job market opportunities for the legal immigrants.{{refn|<ref name=":68">{{cite journal |last1=Marie |first1=Olivier |last2=Pinotti |first2=Paolo |date=2024 |title=Immigration and Crime: An International Perspective == Trends ==
According to migration scientist [[Hein de Haas]] in 2023, "violent crime is decreasing in almost the entire [[Western world]]. In addition, studies show that migrants are actually less criminal on average. This is because first-generation migrants are often people who want to build a new future". De Haas noted an overrepresentation of certain immigrant groups in [[crime statistics]], which he attributed to ethnic profiling and some second-generation immigrants who have no future prospects.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.amnesty.nl/wordt-vervolgd/migratiewetenschapper-hein-de-haas-er-is-helemaal-geen-explosieve-toename-van-migratie |title=Migratiewetenschapper Hein de Haas: 'Er is helemaal geen explosieve toename van migratie'|author=Amnesty |date=15 November 2023|language=nl | quote=Another myth: immigration increases crime. No, says De Haas. 'Violent crime is decreasing in almost the entire Western world. In addition, studies show that migrants are actually less criminal on average. This is because first-generation migrants are often people who want to build a new future. There is certainly overrepresentation of certain groups in crime statistics, but in addition to ethnic profiling, this is mainly a story of some members of the second generation who have no future prospects.'}}</ref>

According to a 2024 article migrants in 30 countries, many (though not the United States, UK, Australia or New Zealand) have higher share of prison populations compared to native-born populations. Among immigrants, younger and less-educated men, as well as those with undocumented or irregular legal status, have a higher [[Propensity probability|propensity]] to commit crimes compared to those with documented status.<ref name=":68" />{{Disputed inline|date=August 2024}}

== Terrorism ==
{{See also|Stochastic terrorism|}}
As of 2020, the relationship between immigration and terrorism was inconclusive.<ref name=":19">{{Cite journal |last1=Helbling |first1=Marc |last2=Meierrieks |first2=Daniel |date=2020 |title=Terrorism and Migration: An Overview |journal=[[British Journal of Political Science]] |language=en |volume=52 |issue=2 |pages=977–996 |doi=10.1017/S0007123420000587 |issn=0007-1234 |quote=1) there is little evidence that more migration unconditionally leads to more terrorist activity, especially in Western countries... (3) the effectiveness of stricter migration policies in deterring terrorism is rather limited |doi-access=free|hdl=10419/228668 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> A 2016 study finds that migrants from terror-prone states increase the risk of terrorism in the host country, but when immigration is not necessarily linked to terrorism in the migrants' countries of origin, immigration is associated with a lower level of terrorism in the host country.<ref name="Induce">{{Cite journal |last1=Bove |first1=Vincenzo |last2=Böhmelt |first2=Tobias |date=2016-02-11 |title=Does Immigration Induce Terrorism? |url=http://repository.essex.ac.uk/17112/1/Bove%20Bohmelt%20JoP.pdf |url-status=live |journal=[[The Journal of Politics]] |volume=78 |issue=2 |pages=572–588 |doi=10.1086/684679 |issn=0022-3816 |s2cid=51947927 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220409014930/http://repository.essex.ac.uk/17112/1/Bove%20Bohmelt%20JoP.pdf |archive-date=9 April 2022 |access-date=18 August 2019}}</ref> The authors note that "only a minority of migrants from high-terrorism states can be associated with increases in terrorism, and not necessarily in a direct way."<ref name="Induce" />

A paper by a group of German political scientists and economists, covering 1980–2010, found that on average, the foreigners were not more likely to become terrorists than the natives.<ref name=":46">{{Cite web |last1=Dreher |first1=Axel |last2=Gassebner |first2=Martin |last3=Schaudt |first3=Paul |date=26 May 2017 |title=The Effect of Migration on Terror – Made at Home or Imported from Abroad? |url=http://cepr.org/active/publications/discussion_papers/dp.php?dpno=12062 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220801031916/https://cepr.org/active/publications/discussion_papers/dp.php?dpno=12062 |archive-date=1 August 2022 |access-date=2017-08-15 |website=[[cepr.org]] |language=en |type=Discussion Paper 12062}}</ref><ref name=":47">{{Cite web |last1=Dreher |first1=Axel |last2=Gassebner |first2=Martin |last3=Schaudt |first3=Paul |date=2017-08-12 |title=Migration and terror |url=http://voxeu.org/article/migration-and-terror |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170815234719/http://voxeu.org/article/migration-and-terror |archive-date=15 August 2017 |access-date=2017-08-15 |website=[[VoxEU.org]]}}</ref> The study also found little evidence that terrorism is systematically imported from predominantly Muslim countries, the exceptions being Algeria and Iran.<ref name=":47" /><ref>{{Cite SSRN|last1=Dreher|first1=Axel|last2=Gassebner|first2=Martin|last3=Schaudt|first3=Paul|date=2017-09-01|title=The Effect of Migration on Terror – Made at Home or Imported from Abroad?|ssrn=2976273}}</ref> High-skilled migrants are associated with a significantly lower risk of terror compared to low-skilled ones, while there is no significant difference between male and female migrants. The study found a risk trade-off: increased immigration laws could decrease the influx of migrants and therefore the potential number of future terrorist attacks, but diminished acceptance by the host country of the migrants increased the terror risk of those already in the country.<ref name=":46" /><ref name=":47" /> Research focusing on the security impact of the [[2015 European migrant crisis|European migrant crisis]] found little to no relationship between increasing migration flows and acts of terrorism.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Forrester |first1=Andrew C. |last2=Powell |first2=Benjamin |last3=Nowrasteh |first3=Alex |last4=Landgrave |first4=Michelangelo |date=2019-08-08 |title=Do immigrants import terrorism? |journal=Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization |volume=166 |pages=529–543 |doi=10.1016/j.jebo.2019.07.019 |issn=0167-2681 |s2cid=202308892}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Treistman|first1=Jeffrey |last2=Gomez |first2=Charles |name-list-style=and|date=2021 | title=European migration and terrorism: humanitarian crisis, political rhetoric, or pragmatic policy? |journal=Conflict, Security & Development|volume=21|issue=3|page=338|doi=10.1080/14678802.2021.1940781|s2cid=236779844 }}</ref>

According to [[Olivier Roy (political scientist)|Olivier Roy]] in 2017 analyzing the previous two decades of terrorism in France, the typical jihadist is a second-generation immigrant or convert who after a period of petty crime was radicalized in prison.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Roy |first=Olivier |date=2017-04-13 |title=Who are the new jihadis? Biographies of 'homegrown' European terrorists show they are violent nihilists who adopt Islam, rather than religious fundamentalists who turn to violence |url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2017/apr/13/who-are-the-new-jihadis |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201101203410/https://www.theguardian.com/news/2017/apr/13/who-are-the-new-jihadis |archive-date=1 November 2020 |access-date=2018-09-24 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> Georgetown University terrorism expert [[Daniel Byman]] agree with Olivier Roy that repression of minority groups, such as Muslims, makes it easier for terrorist organizations to recruit from those minority groups.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Byman |first=Daniel |date=2017-01-30 |title=Why Trump's Policies Will Increase Terrorism&nbsp;– and Why Trump Might Benefit as a Result |url=https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/why-trumps-policies-will-increase-terrorism%e2%80%94and-why-trump-might-benefit-result |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240113183057/https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/why-trumps-policies-will-increase-terrorism%E2%80%94and-why-trump-might-benefit-result |archive-date=13 January 2024 |access-date=2017-08-15 |work=Lawfare |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":67" /> Roy has argued that the [[Burkini|burkini bans]] and [[Laïcité|secularist policies of France]] provoked religious violence in France, which French scholar [[Gilles Kepel]] disputed saying that Britain did not have those policies and still suffered several jihadist attacks in 2017.<ref name=":67">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/13/world/europe/france-radical-islam.html|title='That Ignoramus': 2 French Scholars of Radical Islam Turn Bitter Rivals|work=The New York Times|date=12 July 2016|access-date=2018-07-19|language=en|quote='There is no proof that shows the young men go from Salafism to terrorism,' Mr. Roy said, pointing out that the planner of the Paris attacks in November, Abdelhamid Abaaoud, ate McDonald's, which is not halal. 'None of the terrorists were Salafists.'|last1=Nossiter|first1=Adam|archive-date=12 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210812105230/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/13/world/europe/france-radical-islam.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":310">{{cite news|url=https://www.haaretz.com/world-news/europe/london-gave-shelter-to-radical-islam-and-now-it-s-paying-the-price-1.5482356|title=London Gave Shelter to Radical Islam and Now It's Paying the Price, French Terrorism Expert Says|last=Lerner|first=Davide|date=2017-06-14|work=Haaretz|access-date=2018-06-09|language=en|archive-date=4 May 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220504200920/https://www.haaretz.com/world-news/europe/london-gave-shelter-to-radical-islam-and-now-it-s-paying-the-price-1.5482356}}</ref>{{Update inline|date=August 2024}}

== Hand grenades in Sweden==
Although Swedish police do not record or release the ethnicity{{clarify|reason=This article isn't about ethnicity it's about migration. Should this say migration status?|date=August 2026}}of convicted criminals, there has been a major increase in the number of hand grenade incidents in recent years{{when?|date=August 2026}}.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sturup|first1=Joakim|last2=Gerell|first2=Manne|last3=Rostami|first3=Amir|date=3 January 2019|title=Explosive violence: A near-repeat study of hand grenade detonations and shootings in urban Sweden|journal=European Journal of Criminology|volume=17 |issue=5 |language=en-US|pages=661–677|doi=10.1177/1477370818820656|s2cid=149498600 |issn=1477-3708}}</ref> The explosions are used by gang members to intimidate rival gangs. [[Linda H Staaf]], head of intelligence at [[National Operations Department]], said in 2019 that the perpetrators were from poor areas and many are "perhaps second- or third-generation immigrants".<ref name="bbc.com/news/">{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-50339977|title=Sweden's 100 explosions this year: What's going on?|author=Maddy Savage|location=Stockholm|date=12 November 2019|website=[[BBC]]|access-date=18 November 2019|archive-date=17 November 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191117153015/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-50339977|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Perception ==
{{See also|Fearmongering|Dog whistle (politics)|Sensationalism|Disinformation|Dark figure of crime}}

Research suggests that people overestimate the relationship between immigration and criminality.<ref name=":410"/> Two 2023 studies, one of Switzerland and one of Chile,<ref name=":410" /> have documented how a rise in immigration leads to a rise in fears about immigrant crime without any corresponding rise in crime, with authors of both studies suggesting that media competition led to the overemphasis of immigrant crime narratives and perceptions.<ref name=":68" />

A January 2024 survey in the U.S. found that 57% of Americans believe migrants lead to more crime, which some experts attribute to anecdotal media stories that lack context.<ref name=":65">{{Cite web |last=Shoichet |first=Catherine E. |date=2024-02-15 |title=Analysis: I asked criminologists about immigration and crime in the US. Their answers may surprise you |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/02/15/us/border-migrants-crime-cec/index.html |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hutchinson |first=Bill |date=March 22, 2024 |title=US stats show violent crime dramatically falling, so why is there a rising clash with perception? |url=https://abcnews.go.com/US/us-stats-show-violent-crime-dramatically-falling-rising/story?id=108042096 |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=ABC News |language=en}}</ref> [[Graham Ousey]] believes the perception stems from flashpoint events that politicians use to push up the myth that immigrants create more crime.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Sonnier |first1=Olympia |last2=Haake |first2=Garrett |date=2024-02-29 |title=Trump's claims of a migrant crime wave are not supported by national data |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2024-election/trumps-claims-migrant-crime-wave-are-not-supported-national-data-rcna140896 |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=NBC News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Gomez |first=Alan |title=Mollie Tibbetts murder case: Here are the facts on immigrants committing crimes in US |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2018/08/22/mollie-tibbitts-murder-reignites-debate-over-immigrant-crime/1060792002/ |access-date=2024-08-09 |website=USA TODAY |language=en-US |quote=O'Neil said immigration advocates have not been able to match the Trump administration's rhetoric when framing the immigration debate. She said Trump has been hammering the notion that immigrants are criminals, while Democrats and other immigration supporters have been unable to keep up. As a result, she said the public may associate immigrants with crime, leading to a stereotype that sticks.}}</ref> Donald Trump has been the most prominent promoter of the false link between immigration and crime, according to the [[Associated Press]].<ref name=":66">{{Cite web |last=Spagat |first=Elliot |date=2024-07-16 |title=Donald Trump is the most prominent politician to link immigrants and crime but not the first |url=https://apnews.com/article/immigration-violent-crime-trump-republican-convention-bd40d14546bc7eb9a1dbbadfcb190950 |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=AP News |language=en |quote=Donald Trump has reached the greatest political heights while linking immigration to violent crime, but he's hardly the first American politician to promote the unfounded narrative.}}</ref> Guadalupe Correa-Cabrera argues it is a cornerstone of the MAGA platform.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pinho |first=Faith E. |date=2024-02-27 |title=Immigration rises to top of voters' minds ahead of Super Tuesday, polls find |url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/story/2024-02-27/immigration-rises-to-top-of-voters-minds-ahead-of-super-tuesday-polls-find |access-date=2024-08-08 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US |quote=One of the cornerstones of the MAGA movement, Correa-Cabrera said, is a perception that immigrants bring violence, drugs and insecurity into the United States. Part of the reason, she said, is because many immigrants come to the U.S. to escape violence in their home countries. Still, research has repeatedly debunked the idea that immigrants are more prone to commit violent crime than U.S. citizens.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Debusmann Jr |first=Bernd |date=2024-04-03 |title=Ruby Garcia's family found Trump's comments about her killing 'shocking' |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-68725473 |access-date=2024-08-09 |language=en-GB |quote=Border security, as well as immigration and a perception - not supported by statistics - that it is tied to violent crime, are common features of Mr Trump's rallies and campaign speeches.}}</ref>

A 2016 study of Belgium found that living in an ethnically diverse community led to a greater [[fear of crime]], unrelated to the actual [[crime statistics]].<ref name=":37">{{Cite journal |last1=Hooghe |first1=Marc |last2=de Vroome |first2=Thomas |date=2016-01-01 |title=The relation between ethnic diversity and fear of crime: An analysis of police records and survey data in Belgian communities |journal=International Journal of Intercultural Relations |volume=50 |pages=66–75 |doi=10.1016/j.ijintrel.2015.11.002 |s2cid=133596758 |hdl-access=free |hdl=1874/344394}}</ref> A 2015 study found that the increase in immigration flows into western European countries that took place in the 2000s did "not affect crime victimization, but it is associated with an increase in the fear of crime, the latter being consistently and positively correlated with the natives' unfavourable attitude toward immigrants."<ref name=":5" /> Americans dramatically overestimate the relationship between refugees and terrorism.<ref name=":38">{{Cite news |date=2016-06-28 |title=America's puzzling moral ambivalence about Middle East refugees |language=en-US |publisher=Brookings Institution |url=https://www.brookings.edu/blog/markaz/2016/06/28/americas-puzzling-moral-ambivalence-about-middle-east-refugees/ |access-date=2017-01-26 |archive-date=28 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170128185600/https://www.brookings.edu/blog/markaz/2016/06/28/americas-puzzling-moral-ambivalence-about-middle-east-refugees/ |url-status=live }}</ref> A 2018 study found that media coverage of immigrants in the United States has a general tendency to emphasize illegality and/or criminal behavior in a way that is inconsistent with actual immigrant demographics.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2018|title=Picturing immigration: how the media criminalizes immigrants|journal=Politics, Groups, and Identities|volume=6|issue=4|pages=814–824|doi=10.1080/21565503.2018.1484375|last1=Farris|first1=Emily M.|last2=Silber Mohamed|first2=Heather|s2cid=158047679}}</ref> A study of coverage of refugees in the ''Guardian'' and the ''Times'' in the UK from 2015 to 2018 found that media portrayals made Muslim refugees seem like threats to the economy or security and exaggerated differences between these refugees and the native population.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Połońska-Kimunguyi |first=Ewa |date=2022-01-06 |title=Echoes of Empire: racism and historical amnesia in the British media coverage of migration |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-021-01020-4 |journal=Humanities and Social Sciences Communications |language=en |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=1–13 |article-number=3 |doi=10.1057/s41599-021-01020-4  |doi-access=free|issn=2662-9992}}</ref>

''[[The Economist]]'' reported in 2018 that some right-wing parties make claims about a connection between immigration and crime, even though the issues are mostly unrelated.<ref name=":69">{{Cite news |date=June 30, 2018 |title=Confusion over immigration and crime is roiling European politics |url=https://www.economist.com/europe/2018/06/30/confusion-over-immigration-and-crime-is-roiling-european-politics |access-date=2024-07-28 |newspaper=The Economist |issn=0013-0613 |quote=Europe's immigration problems and its crime problems are mostly unrelated. But they are inseparable in politics...Male refugees are committing fewer crimes as they move out of shelters, where fights break out. It also helps that the share of women among the migrants is rising. 'The biggest factor in reducing violence is if the number of women goes up,' says Mr Pfeiffer. 'The young husbands suddenly care about their family.'}}</ref>

== Politics ==
Research suggests that the perception that there is a positive causal link between immigration and crime leads to greater support for anti-immigration policies or parties.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Does Crime Pay? Issue Ownership, Political Opportunity, and the Populist Right in Western Europe |journal = Comparative Political Studies|date = 2010-11-01|issn = 0010-4140|pages = 1471–1498|volume = 43|issue = 11|doi = 10.1177/0010414010372593|first = Jason Matthew|last = Smith|s2cid = 154607509}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Crime Story: The role of crime and immigration in the anti-immigration vote |journal = Electoral Studies|date = 2011-12-01|pages = 658–671|volume = 30|issue = 4|doi = 10.1016/j.electstud.2011.06.010|first1 = Elias|last1 = Dinas|first2 = Joost|last2 = van Spanje}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Owning the issues of crime and immigration: The relation between immigration and crime news and anti-immigrant voting in 11 countries|journal = Electoral Studies|date = 2015-06-01|pages = 59–69|volume = 38|doi = 10.1016/j.electstud.2015.03.001|first1 = Bjorn|last1 = Burscher|first2 = Joost|last2 = van Spanje|first3 = Claes H.|last3 = de Vreese|s2cid = 59143838|url = https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/2563200/168937_503146.pdf|access-date = 19 December 2020|archive-date = 27 April 2021|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210427175418/https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/2563200/168937_503146.pdf|url-status = live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|title = Immigration sceptics, xenophobes or racists? Radical right-wing voting in six West European countries |journal = European Journal of Political Research|date = 2008-10-01|issn = 1475-6765|pages = 737–765|volume = 47|issue = 6|doi = 10.1111/j.1475-6765.2008.00784.x|first = Jens|last = Rydgren}}</ref> Research also suggests a vicious cycle of bigotry and immigrant alienation could exacerbate immigrant criminality and bigotry. For instance, UC San Diego political scientist [[Claire Adida]], [[Stanford University]] political scientist [[David D. Laitin|David Laitin]], and Sorbonne University economist Marie-Anne Valfort argue: <blockquote>[F]ear-based policies that target groups of people according to their religion or region of origin are counter-productive. Our own research, which explains the failed integration of Muslim immigrants in France, suggests that such policies can feed into a vicious cycle that damages national security. French Islamophobia—a response to cultural difference—has encouraged Muslim immigrants to withdraw from French society, which then feeds back into French Islamophobia, thus further exacerbating Muslims' alienation, and so on. Indeed, the failure of French security in 2015 was likely due to police tactics that intimidated rather than welcomed the children of immigrants—an approach that makes it hard to obtain crucial information from community members about potential threats.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Adida|first1=Claire L.|last2=Laitin|first2=David D.|last3=Valfort|first3=Marie-Anne|date=2017-02-01|title=The Wrong Way to Stop Terrorism|url=https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/2017-02-01/wrong-way-stop-terrorism|journal=Foreign Affairs|access-date=4 February 2017|archive-date=5 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170205104415/https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/2017-02-01/wrong-way-stop-terrorism|url-status=live}}</ref></blockquote>A study of the long-run effects of the 9/11 terrorist attacks found that the post-9/11 increase in [[hate crime]]s against Muslims decreased assimilation by Muslim immigrants.<ref name="Gould n/a-n/a">{{Cite journal|title = The Long-run Effect of 9/11: Terrorism, Backlash, and the Assimilation of Muslim Immigrants in the West |journal = The Economic Journal|volume = 126|issue = 597|date = 2015-07-01|issn = 1468-0297|pages = 2064–2114|doi = 10.1111/ecoj.12219|first1 = Eric D.|last1 = Gould|first2 = Esteban F.|last2 = Klor|s2cid = 55809315|hdl = 10.1111/ecoj.12219|hdl-access = free}}</ref> Controlling for relevant factors, the authors found that "Muslim immigrants living in states with the sharpest increase in hate crimes also exhibit: greater chances of marrying within their own ethnic group; higher fertility; lower female labour force participation; and lower English proficiency."<ref name="Gould n/a-n/a"/> Hate crimes and [[family separation]] have also been consequences of rhetoric linking crime to [[Mexico–United States border crisis|migration from Mexico]].<ref name=":65" />

States that experience terrorist acts on their own soil or against their own citizens are more likely to adopt stricter restrictions on asylum recognition.<ref>{{Cite journal|title = Do asylum recognition rates in Europe respond to transnational terrorism? The migration-security nexus revisited |journal = European Union Politics|date = 2014-12-01|issn = 1465-1165|pages = 445–471|volume = 15|issue = 4|doi = 10.1177/1465116514534908|language = en|first = Nazli|last = Avdan|s2cid = 154649714}}</ref> Individuals who believe that African Americans and Hispanics are more prone to violence are more likely to support capital punishment.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Unnever|first1=James D.|last2=Cullen|first2=Francis T.|date=2012-11-01|title=White Perceptions of Whether African Americans and Hispanics are Prone to Violence and Support for the Death Penalty |journal=Journal of Research in Crime and Delinquency|language=en|volume=49|issue=4|pages=519–544|doi=10.1177/0022427811415533|s2cid=146774838|issn=0022-4278}}</ref> The [[Dillingham Commission]] singled out immigrants from Southern Europe for their involvement in violent crime (even though the data did not support its conclusions).<ref name=":28" /><ref name=":66" /> The commission's overall findings provided the rationale for sweeping 1920s [[immigration reduction|immigration-reduction]] acts, including the ''[[Emergency Quota Act]]'' of 1921, which favored immigration from [[Northern Europe|northern]] and [[western Europe]] by restricting the annual number of immigrants from any given country to 3 percent of the total number of people from that country living in the United States in 1910. The movement for immigration restriction that the Dillingham Commission helped to stimulate culminated in the [[National Origins Formula]], part of the [[Immigration Act of 1924|''Immigration Act'' of 1924]], which capped national immigration at 150,000 annually and completely barred immigration from [[Asia]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://ocp.hul.harvard.edu/immigration/dillingham.html |title=Open Collections Program: Immigration to the US, Dillingham Commission (1907-1910)<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=9 January 2016 |archive-date=25 January 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130125123555/http://ocp.hul.harvard.edu/immigration/dillingham.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Asia ==
=== Japan ===
{{Further|Demographics of Japan|Crime in Japan}}

A survey of existing research on immigration and crime in Japan found that "prosecution and sentencing in Japan do seem to result in some disparities by nationality, but the available data are too limited to arrive at confident conclusions about their nature or magnitude".<ref>{{Cite book|title = Convergence of Control – Oxford Handbooks|url = http://oxfordhandbooks.com/view/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199859016.001.0001/oxfordhb-9780199859016-e-012|doi = 10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199859016.013.012|first1 = Ryoko|last1 = Yamamoto|first2 = David|last2 = Johnson|year = 2014|isbn = 978-0-19-985901-6|access-date = 26 January 2016|archive-date = 19 June 2021|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210619123328/https://www.oxfordhandbooks.com/view/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780199859016.001.0001/oxfordhb-9780199859016-e-012|url-status = live}}</ref> According to a 1997 news report, a large portion of crimes by immigrants are by [[Chinese people in Japan|Chinese in Japan]], and some highly publicized crimes by organized groups of Chinese (often with help of [[Yakuza|Japanese organized crime]]) have led to a negative public perception of immigrants.<ref name="worries">{{cite news|title=Japan Worries About a Trend: Crime by Chinese|work=[[The New York Times]]|date=March 12, 1997|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/03/12/world/japan-worries-about-a-trend-crime-by-chinese.html|first=Sheryl|last=Wudunn|access-date=April 30, 2010|archive-date=27 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171227174525/http://www.nytimes.com/1997/03/12/world/japan-worries-about-a-trend-crime-by-chinese.html|url-status=live}}</ref> According to the [[National Police Agency (Japan)|National Police Agency]] in 2015, [[Vietnamese people in Japan|Vietnamese nationals]] overtook Chinese as having the highest number of criminal offenses for foreigners.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2016-11-27|title=Change to the power map of foreign crime? Vietnamese criminal offenders overtake Chinese|url=https://www.sankei.com/article/20161127-JVMSVDKNAVPBZEQKQYJJJKLI6A/|access-date=2022-01-05|website=[[Sankei Shimbun]]|language=ja|archive-date=5 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220105085836/https://www.sankei.com/article/20161127-JVMSVDKNAVPBZEQKQYJJJKLI6A/|url-status=live}}</ref> The number of offenses has reportedly been on the rise as of 2021,<ref>{{Cite web|date=November 20, 2020|title=Increasingly desperate Vietnamese blamed for surging crime wave|url=https://japantoday.com/category/features/kuchikomi/Increasingly-desperate-Vietnamese-blamed-for-surging-crime-wave|url-status=live|archive-url=https://archive.today/20220104172712/https://japantoday.com/category/features/kuchikomi/Increasingly-desperate-Vietnamese-blamed-for-surging-crime-wave?comment-order=oldest|archive-date=January 4, 2022|website=[[Japan Today]]|language=en|access-date=January 5, 2022}}</ref> and has been linked to the lower economic status of Vietnamese in Japan.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-04-08|title=Japanese police investigated 2,889 foreign trainees in 2020|url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2021/04/08/national/trainees-crime-statistics/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210408125026/http://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2021/04/08/national/trainees-crime-statistics/|archive-date=2021-04-08|website=[[The Japan Times]]|language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Malaysia ===
A 2017 study found that immigration to Malaysia decreases [[property crime]] rates and violent crime rates.<ref name=":45">{{Cite journal|last1=Ozden|first1=Caglar|last2=Testaverde|first2=Mauro|last3=Wagner|first3=Mathis|title=How and Why Does Immigration Affect Crime? Evidence from Malaysia|journal=The World Bank Economic Review|volume=32|pages=183–202|doi=10.1093/wber/lhx010|year=2018|hdl=10986/32171|hdl-access=free}}</ref> In the case of property crime rates, this is in part because immigrants improve economic conditions for natives.<ref name=":45" />

==Europe==
{{further|Immigration to Europe|List of countries by immigrant population}}Most studies fail to show any [[Causality|causal effect]] of immigration on overall crime rates.<ref name=":70" /><ref name=":71" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name="NewEvidence" /><ref name=":6" /><ref name=":4abc" /><ref name=":21" /><ref name="CrimeInEurope2011" /><ref name=":7" /> A 2015 study found that the increase in immigration flows into western European countries that took place in the 2000s did "not affect crime victimization, but it is associated with an increase in the [[fear of crime]], the latter being consistently and positively correlated with the natives' unfavourable attitude toward immigrants."<ref name=":5" /> In a survey of the existing economic literature on immigration and crime, one economist describes the existing literature in 2014 as showing that "the results for Europe are mixed for property crime but no association is found for violent crime".<ref name=":8" />

=== Denmark ===
{{Further|Immigration to Denmark|Crime in Denmark}}
[[File:Denmark male crime index by country of origin.png|left|thumb|247x247px|Crime index of males in Denmark by country of origin <ref>{{Cite web |title=Publikation: Indvandrere i Danmark 2025 |url=https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/Udgivelser/GetPubFile.aspx?id=54707&sid=__samlet%20publikation%202025 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260629071158/https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/Udgivelser/GetPubFile.aspx?id=54707&sid=__samlet%20publikation%202025 |archive-date=29 June 2026 |access-date=22 September 2026 |website=dst.dk |page=114 |language=Danish}}</ref>]]
Descendants of non-Western immigrants are significantly overrepresented in criminal statistics, especially in violent crimes, traffic violations, and certain sexual offenses.

A 2019 report by the Danish {{ill|Crime Prevention Council|dk|Det Kriminalpræventive Råd}} reviewed 12 studies and came to the conclusion that it is likely that adults under 30 with an ethnic minority background are overrepresented in crime statistics. It noted methodological differences between the studies making it hard to draw definitive conclusions.<ref>{{cite web |title=Kriminalitet og etniske minoriteter |url=https://dkr.dk/media/7016/kriminalitet-og-etniske-minoriteter-pixi-080219.pdf |website=The Crime Prevention Council |page=2 |language=da}}</ref>

A 2019 study reviewing ten studies on the relationship between immigration and crime in Denmark found that different studies came to different conclusions as to whether immigrants were overrepresented, depending on what kind of data was used.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Klement |first=Christian |date=2019-12-09 |title=Studies of immigrant crime in Denmark |journal=Nordic Journal of Criminology |language=en |volume=21 |pages=11–31 |doi=10.1080/2578983X.2019.1702270 |issn=2578-983X |s2cid=214021598}}</ref>

Immigrants who have committed crimes may be denied [[Danish nationality law|Danish citizenship]]. For instance, immigrants who have received a prison sentence of one year or more, or at least three months for crimes against a person cannot receive citizenship. Convictions which have resulted in a fine also carries with it a time period for immigrants, where citizenship applications are rejected up to 4.5 years after the fine. Upon several offences, the period is extended by 3 years.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Kriminalitet — Udlændinge- og Integrationsministeriet|url=https://uim.dk/arbejdsomrader/statsborgerskab/udenlandske-statsborgere/betingelser/kriminalitet|access-date=2020-12-20|website=uim.dk|archive-date=2020-11-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112031803/https://uim.dk/arbejdsomrader/statsborgerskab/udenlandske-statsborgere/betingelser/kriminalitet}}</ref> In the 2018-2020 period, 83 people were denied [[Danish nationality law|Danish citizenship]] because they had committed a serious crime. Among those were people who had received court sentences for gang crime, violence against children and sexual offenses. People who have received a prison sentence of at least one year are barred from receiving citizenship, along with people who have received a prison sentence of at least three months for a crime against a person.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-08-14 |title=83 kriminelle udlændinge udelukket fra dansk statsborgerskab |url=https://www.dr.dk/nyheder/politik/83-kriminelle-udlaendinge-udelukket-fra-dansk-statsborgerskab |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200815233612/https://www.dr.dk/nyheder/politik/83-kriminelle-udlaendinge-udelukket-fra-dansk-statsborgerskab |archive-date=15 August 2020 |access-date=2020-08-16 |website=DR |language=da-DK}}</ref> In April 2021, the [[Frederiksen I Cabinet|Mette Frederiksen Cabinet]] approved regulation which stops awarding citizenship to foreigners who had received a prison sentence in court which also encompassed suspended prison sentences. Previously, awarding citizenship was possible for foreigners with a prison sentence of less than a year.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jensen |first=Henrik |date=2021-04-20 |title=Fængselsdømte udelukkes fra at få statsborgerskab: "Vi bliver nødt til at trække en streg i sandet" |url=https://www.berlingske.dk/content/item/1557406 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240224084437/https://www.berlingske.dk/politik/faengselsdoemte-udelukkes-fra-at-faa-statsborgerskab-vi-bliver-noedt-til |archive-date=24 February 2024 |access-date=2021-04-21 |website=Berlingske.dk |language=da}}</ref> One study of Denmark found that providing immigrants with voting rights reduced their crime rate.<ref>{{Cite SSRN |title=Democratic Involvement and Immigrants' Compliance with the Law |last1=Slotwinski |first1=Michaela |last2=Stutzer |first2=Alois |date=2017-02-27 |ssrn=2923633 |last3=Gorinas |first3=Cédric}}</ref>

A report by [[Statistics Denmark]] released in December 2015 found that 83% of crimes are committed by individuals of Danish origin (88% of the total population), 14% by individuals of non-Western descent and 3% by those of non-Danish Western descent. An index standardized for age shows that crime rates are 48% higher among male immigrants and 140% higher among male descendants of immigrants.<ref name="StatsDenmark">{{Cite web |date=2015 |title=Indvandrere i Danmark 2015 |trans-title=Immigrants in Denmark 2015 |url=http://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/Udgivelser/GetPubFile.aspx?id=20703&sid=indv2015 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160215235233/http://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/Udgivelser/GetPubFile.aspx?id=20703&sid=indv2015 |archive-date=15 February 2016 |access-date=2019-04-18 |publisher=Statistics Denmark |pages=93,100 & others |language=da}}</ref>{{Original research inline|date=August 2024}}{{Primary source inline|date=August 2024}} At 4%, male migrants aged 15–64 with non-Western backgrounds had twice the [[conviction rate]] against the [[Danish Penal Code]] in 2018, compared to 2% for Danish men. In a given year, about 13% of all male descendants of non-Western migrants aged 17–24 are convicted against the penal code.<ref>{{Cite news |title=GRAFIK Indvandrede og efterkommere halter efter etniske danskere |url=https://www.dr.dk/ligetil/grafik-indvandrede-og-efterkommere-halter-efter-etniske-danskere |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180714153842/https://www.dr.dk/ligetil/grafik-indvandrede-og-efterkommere-halter-efter-etniske-danskere |archive-date=14 July 2018 |access-date=2018-07-14 |work=[[Danish Broadcasting Corporation]] |language=da}}</ref> In 2017, 30% of the prison population were foreign nationals with the largest group being Romanian citizens, followed by Turkish. and Lithuanian citizens. On 1 July 2017, there were 3403 inmates and 2382 of those were Danish citizens.<ref name="DR2017">{{Cite web |date=7 July 2017 |title=Fængselsformand: Udenlandske indsatte udfordrer os helt vildt |url=https://www.dr.dk/nyheder/indland/faengselsformand-udenlandske-indsatte-udfordrer-os-helt-vildt |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191003062014/https://www.dr.dk/nyheder/indland/faengselsformand-udenlandske-indsatte-udfordrer-os-helt-vildt |archive-date=3 October 2019 |access-date=2019-10-03 |website=DR |language=da-DK}}</ref>

A 2014 study of the random dispersal of refugee immigrants over the period 1986–1998, and focusing on the immigrant children who underwent this random assignment before the age of 15, suggests that exposure to neighbourhood crime increases individual crime propensity.<ref name=":31" /> The share of convicted criminals living in the assignment neighborhood at assignment affects later crime convictions of males, but not of females, who were assigned to these neighborhoods as children.<ref name=":31" /> The authors "find that a one standard deviation increase in the share of youth criminals living in the assignment neighborhood, and who committed a crime in the assignment year, increases the probability of a conviction for male assignees by between 5 percent and 9 percent later in life (when they are between 15 and 21 years old)."<ref name=":31" />

In late 2020, the [[Minister for Integration (Denmark)|minister for Immigration and Integration]], [[Mattias Tesfaye]], announced that the category "Non-Western immigrant" in Danish statistics on immigrants was to be changed where immigrants with higher rates of crime and unemployment were to be placed into the MENAPT category encompassing immigrants from the Middle East, North Africa, Pakistan and Turkey. This was due to the "Non-Western" category encompassed major differences as integration of immigrants from Thailand, the Philippines and Latin America was markedly different from those of the Middle East. Of the about 500 thousand immigrants and second-generation immigrants in Denmark, 54.5 percent came from [[MENAPT]] countries. Statistics showed that young males from MENAPT countries had markedly higher crime rates than the corresponding group from other non-Western countries, where 4.6% had been sentenced for crimes while from other non-Western countries the rate was 1.8%.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Birk|first=Christian|date=2020-12-13|title=Tesfaye afviser kritik af nye "stigmatiserende" udlændingetal: "Jeg synes ikke, det er racistisk at kategorisere lande"|url=https://www.berlingske.dk/content/item/1526243|access-date=2020-12-20|website=[[Berlingske]]|language=da|archive-date=24 February 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240224084517/https://www.berlingske.dk/danmark/tesfaye-afviser-kritik-af-nye-stigmatiserende-udlaendingetal-jeg-synes|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Finland===
{{Further|Immigration to Finland|Crime in Finland}}
Immigrant [[crime in Finland]] became a topic of public debate in the 1990s-early 21st century period with the arrivals of [[Somalis in Finland]].<ref name="is20181215">{{Cite web|url=https://www.is.fi/kotimaa/art-2000005933247.html|title=Iso selvitys ulkomaalaisten seksuaalirikollisuudesta – määrät, syyt, ratkaisukeinot|last1=Viljakainen|first1=Miika|last2=Lakka|first2=Päivi|date=2018-12-15|website=Ilta-Sanomat|language=fi|access-date=2018-12-21|quote=Maahanmuuttajien rikollisuus nousi puheenaiheeksi 1990-luvun alussa, kun ensimmäiset somalit tulivat Suomeen ja itärikollisuuden pelättiin räjähtävän käsiin.|archive-date=21 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181221060257/https://www.is.fi/kotimaa/art-2000005933247.html|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Verify source|date=August 2024}}

In 1998, 10 times more "foreign-looking" men were accused of rape than the overall percentage of foreigners in Finland, which the Chief Inspector interviewed explained that at least part of that disparity could be because, "It may be that a Finnish woman regards it as more of a crime when the perpetrator is foreign. If the rapist is a Finn, the woman might perhaps think more about her own role in what has happened."<ref name=":55">{{cite web |author=Partanen |first=Anu |author-link=Anu Partanen |date=August 22, 2000 |title=Foreigners figure high in rape statistics: Threshold lower for women to report rapes by non-Finns |url=http://www2.hs.fi/english/archive/news.asp?id=20000822xx3 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120314011946/http://www2.hs.fi/english/archive/news.asp?id=20000822xx3 |archive-date=2012-03-14 |website=[[Helsingin Sanomat]] |quote=When the victims file their accusations, as many as 17% of the women involved believed the rapist to be of foreign extraction. This is a pretty huge figure, given that there are only some 85,000 foreigners living in Finland, or just 1.65% of the population. The figures do not tell the whole story, however. The police receive slightly fewer than 500 reports of rape annually, but experts have estimated that the yearly total of rapes is in the thousands, perhaps even the tens of thousands of women. The great majority of rapists are the Finnish relatives, friends, and acquaintances of Finnish victims, and crimes committed by such persons are not generally reported to the police.}}</ref>

A 2015 study found that immigrant youth had higher incidence rates in 14 out of 17 delinquent acts. The gap is small for thefts and vandalism, and no significant differences for [[shoplifting]], bullying and use of intoxicants. According to the authors, "weak parental [[social control]] and risk routines, such as staying out late, appear to partly explain the immigrant youths' higher delinquency", and "the relevance of socioeconomic factors was modest".<ref name=":53">{{Cite journal |last1=Salmi |first1=Venla |last2=Kivivuori |first2=Janne |last3=Aaltonen |first3=Mikko |date=2015-11-01 |title=Correlates of immigrant youth crime in Finland |journal=[[European Journal of Criminology]] |volume=12 |issue=6 |pages=681–699 |doi=10.1177/1477370815587768 |issn=1477-3708 |s2cid=142551581}}</ref>

According to 2014 official statistics, 24% of rapes are estimated to have been committed by individuals with foreign surnames in Finland.<ref>{{cite web |last=Danielsson |first=Petri |title=Rikollisuustilanne 2019 rikollisuuskehitys tilastojen ja tutkimusten valossa |url=https://helda.helsinki.fi/server/api/core/bitstreams/fe2cf972-a5cd-4e37-9e55-5c3515ccdd29/content |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160625143210/https://helda.helsinki.fi/bitstream/handle/10138/156334/Katsauksia_4_Rikollisuustilanne_2014_2015.pdf |archive-date=25 June 2016 |access-date=10 February 2016 |publisher=University of Helsinki - Institute of Criminology and Legal Policy |page=88 |language=fi |issn=2342-7779}}</ref>{{Verify source|date=August 2024}}{{Update inline|date=August 2024}}{{Primary source inline|date=August 2024}} <!-- Foreign-language speakers and the foreign-born comprised roughly 6% of the Finnish population in 2014, meaning that the percentage of individuals with foreign surnames in Finland.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.intermin.fi/en/migration/immigration_to_finland|title=Immigration to Finland|publisher=Ministry of the Interior|website=www.intermin.fi|access-date=2016-06-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160609065534/http://www.intermin.fi/en/migration/immigration_to_finland|archive-date=2016-06-09}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.stat.fi/til/vaerak/2015/vaerak_2015_2016-04-01_en.pdf|title=Number of persons speaking national languages as their native language went down for the second year in a row|access-date=9 June 2016|archive-date=28 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160628053619/http://www.stat.fi/til/vaerak/2015/vaerak_2015_2016-04-01_en.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Verification needed|date=August 2024}} -->

===France===
{{Further|Immigration to France|Crime in France}}

A 2006 study found "that the share of immigrants in the population has no significant impact on crime rates once immigrants' economic circumstances are controlled for, while finding that unemployed immigrants tend to commit more crimes than unemployed non-immigrants."<ref name=":29">{{Cite journal|title = Are immigrants more likely to commit crimes? Evidence from France |journal = Applied Economics Letters|date = 2009-10-01|issn = 1350-4851|pages = 1537–1541|volume = 16|issue = 15|doi = 10.1080/13504850701578892|first1 = Yu|last1 = Aoki|first2 = Yasuyuki|last2 = Todo|s2cid = 154177816}}</ref> As shown in the 2006 study with 1999 French census data calculations, an unemployed nonimmigrant outlier raises the number of crimes by 0.297, and another raises it by 0.546.<ref name=":29" />

Aoki and Yasuyuki's research show that data that is frequently shown regarding French immigration and crime is misleading, as it does not take discrimination and economic hardships into account as a motivator for criminal acts. As shown in the 2006 study, after adding the share of unemployed immigrants in the labor force, it is determined that the effect of the share of immigrants now becomes insignificant.<ref name=":29" />

With the exception of 2015 in Macrotrends collection of data, French crime rates overall have been on the steady decline, experiencing a 5.68% decline from 2017 to 2018.<ref name=":52" /> However, immigration rates are on the incline, with a 10.74% increase of migrants granted asylum from 2017 to 2018. This data from 1990 to 2022 indicates that crime rates and migration rates do not correlate if one is only looking at the numbers, with no other qualitative factors in place.<ref name=":52">{{Cite web |title=France Refugee Statistics 1960-2022 |url=https://www.macrotrends.net/countries/FRA/france/refugee-statistics |access-date=2022-03-30 |website=www.macrotrends.net |archive-date=27 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220127034510/https://www.macrotrends.net/countries/FRA/france/refugee-statistics |url-status=live }}</ref>

A study by sociologist [[:fr:Farhad Khosrokhavar|Farhad Khosrokhavar]], director of studies at the [[School for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences|EHESS]], found that "Muslims, mostly from North African origin, are becoming the most numerous group in [French prisons]."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://stanford.edu/dept/france-stanford/Conferences/Islam/Khosrokhavar.pdf|title=Anti-Semitism of the Muslims in France: the case of the prisoners|last=Khosrokhavar|first=Farhad|date=5 July 2016|website=Stanford University|access-date=5 July 2016|archive-date=24 February 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210224193450/https://stanford.edu/dept/france-stanford/Conferences/Islam/Khosrokhavar.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=L'islam dans les prisons|last=Khosrokhavar|first=Farhad|publisher=Editions Balland|year=2004|isbn=978-2-7158-1493-6|location=Paris}}</ref> His work has been criticized for taking into account only 160 prisoners in 4 prisons, all close to northern Paris where most immigrants live.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.franceinfo.fr/emission/le-vrai-du-faux/2014-2015/60-des-detenus-francais-sont-musulmans-25-01-2015-15-46|title=60% des détenus français sont musulmans ?|date=2015-01-25|work=Franceinfo|access-date=2017-08-27|language=fr-FR|archive-date=19 November 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151119094637/http://www.franceinfo.fr/emission/le-vrai-du-faux/2014-2015/60-des-detenus-francais-sont-musulmans-25-01-2015-15-46|url-status=live}}</ref>

According to police figures, 77% of perpetrators of solved rapes in Paris during 2023 were of foreign nationality.<ref name="q166">{{cite web | title=INFO EUROPE 1 – Les étrangers à l'origine de 77% des viols élucidés dans les rues de Paris en 2023 | website=europe1.fr | date=2024-04-18 | url=https://www.europe1.fr/Police-Justice/info-europe-1-les-etrangers-a-lorigine-de-77-des-viols-commis-dans-les-rues-de-paris-en-2023-4242136 | language=fr | access-date=2025-03-10}}</ref>

===Germany===
{{main|Immigration and crime in Germany}}
Published in 2017, the first comprehensive study of the social effects of the one million refugees going to Germany found that it caused "very small increases in crime in particular with respect to drug offenses and fare-dodging."<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://qz.com/901076/what-effect-did-the-record-influx-of-refugees-have-on-jobs-and-crime-in-germany-not-much/|title=What effect did the record influx of refugees have on jobs and crime in Germany? Not much|last=Mohdin|first=Aamna|work=Quartz|access-date=2017-02-03|language=en-US|archive-date=4 February 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170204005806/https://qz.com/901076/what-effect-did-the-record-influx-of-refugees-have-on-jobs-and-crime-in-germany-not-much/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite SSRN|last1=Gehrsitz|first1=Markus|last2=Ungerer|first2=Martin|date=2017-01-01|title=Jobs, Crime, and Votes: A Short-Run Evaluation of the Refugee Crisis in Germany|ssrn=2903116}}</ref> A 2021 study found that asylum seekers had no impact on violent [[crime in Germany]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Dehos|first=Fabiant|date=2021-01-06|title=The Refugee Wave to Germany and Its Impact on Crime|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166046220303252|journal=Regional Science and Urban Economics|language=en|volume=88|article-number=103640|doi=10.1016/j.regsciurbeco.2020.103640|bibcode=2021RSUE...88j3640D |issn=0166-0462|via=|hdl=10419/175407|s2cid=158438190|hdl-access=free}}</ref> A 2019 study by [[Otto von Guericke University Magdeburg]] economists found that the arrival of nearly one million refugees in 2015 did not increase the likelihood that Germans would be the victims of crime.<ref>{{Cite SSRN|last1=Kvasnicka|first1=Michael|last2=Huang|first2=Yue|date=2019-07-01|title=Immigration and Crimes Against Natives: The 2015 Refugee Crisis in Germany|language=en|ssrn=3427607}}</ref>

A January 2018 [[Zurich University of Applied Sciences]] study commissioned by the German government attributed over 90% of a 10% overall rise in violent crime from to 2015 to 2016 in Lower Saxony to refugees.<ref name="TheLocal2018">{{Cite news |date=2018-01-03 |title=Prevention improvement is solution to refugee crime, study finds |url=https://www.thelocal.de/20180103/prevention-improvement-is-solution-to-refugee-crime-study-finds |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180619213759/https://www.thelocal.de/20180103/prevention-improvement-is-solution-to-refugee-crime-study-finds |archive-date=19 June 2018 |access-date=2018-06-19 |work=the local de |language=en}}</ref> The study's authors noted that there were great differences between different refugee groups.<ref name="Reuters2018">{{cite news |last1=Alkousaa |first1=Riham |date=2018-01-03 |title=Violent crime rises in Germany and is attributed to refugees |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-europe-migrants-germany-crime/violent-crime-rises-in-germany-and-is-attributed-to-refugees-idUSKBN1ES16J |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210203173723/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-europe-migrants-germany-crime/violent-crime-rises-in-germany-and-is-attributed-to-refugees-idUSKBN1ES16J |archive-date=3 February 2021 |access-date=19 June 2018 |work=Reuters}}</ref> Refugees from [[North Africa]]n countries [[Algeria]], [[Tunisia]] and [[Moroccans in Germany|Morocco]] constituted 0.9% of refugees but represented 17.1% of violent crime refugee suspects and 31% of robbery refugee suspects. The latter corresponds to a 35-fold over-representation. Refugees from Afghanistan, Syria and Iraq represented 54.7% of the total, but represented 16% of refugee robbery suspects and 34.9% violent crime suspects and were thus underrepresented.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Zur Entwicklung der Gewalt in Deutschland|last1=Pfeiffer |first1=Christian |last2=Baier |first2=Dirk |last3=Kliem |first3=Sören |date=3 January 2018|publisher=[[Zürcher Fachhochschule]]|page=2|language=de}}</ref>

A report released by the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation in November 2015 found that over the period January–September 2015, the crime rate of refugees was the same as that of native Germans.<ref name=":18">{{Cite web|url=http://www.dw.com/en/report-refugees-have-not-increased-crime-rate-in-germany/a-18848890|title=Report: refugees have not increased crime rate in Germany|date=2015-11-13|website=Deutsche Welle|access-date=2016-01-26|archive-date=4 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160204161530/http://www.dw.com/en/report-refugees-have-not-increased-crime-rate-in-germany/a-18848890|url-status=live}}</ref> According to [[Deutsche Welle]], the report "concluded that the majority of crimes committed by refugees (67 percent) consisted of theft, robbery and fraud. Sex crimes made for less than 1 percent of all crimes committed by refugees, while homicide registered the smallest fraction at 0.1 percent."<ref name=":18" /> According to the conservative newspaper [[Die Welt]]'s description of the report, the most common crime committed by refugees was not paying fares on public transportation.<ref>13.11.15 Straftaten "im sehr niedrigen sechsstelligen Bereich", Die Welt, https://www.welt.de/politik/deutschland/article148812603/Straftaten-im-sehr-niedrigen-sechsstelligen-Bereich.html {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170830021844/https://www.welt.de/politik/deutschland/article148812603/Straftaten-im-sehr-niedrigen-sechsstelligen-Bereich.html |date=30 August 2017 }}</ref> According to Deutsche Welle's reporting in February 2016 of a report by the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation, the number of crimes committed by refugees did not rise in proportion to the number of refugees between 2014 and 2015.<ref name=":32">{{Cite web|url=http://www.dw.com/en/report-refugee-related-crimes-in-germany-increase-less-than-influx-of-asylum-seekers/a-19053227|title=Report: Refugee-related crimes in Germany increase less than influx of asylum seekers {{!}} NRS-Import|date=2016-02-17|website=Deutsche Welle|access-date=2016-04-28|archive-date=30 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160430100331/http://www.dw.com/en/report-refugee-related-crimes-in-germany-increase-less-than-influx-of-asylum-seekers/a-19053227|url-status=live}}</ref> According to Deutsche Welle, "between 2014 and 2015, the number of crimes committed by refugees increased by 79 percent. Over the same period the number of refugees in Germany increased by 440 percent."<ref name=":32" />

The U.S. fact-checker [[PolitiFact]] noted that Germany's crime data suggests that the crime rate of the average refugee is lower than that of the average German.<ref name=":33">{{Cite web |last=Emery Jr. |first=C. Eugene |date=May 11, 2016 |title=Donald Trump says Germany now riddled with crime thanks to refugees |url=http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/statements/2016/may/11/donald-trump/donald-trump-says-germany-now-riddled-crime-thanks/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160512114519/http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/statements/2016/may/11/donald-trump/donald-trump-says-germany-now-riddled-crime-thanks/ |archive-date=12 May 2016 |access-date=2016-05-12 |website=PolitiFact}}</ref> In April 2017, the crime figures released for 2016 showed that the number of suspected crimes by refugees, asylum-seekers and illegal immigrants increased by 50 percent.<ref name=":44">{{cite news |title=Migrant crime in Germany rises by 50 per cent, new figures show |website=[[The Daily Telegraph]] |date=25 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230613050012/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2017/04/25/migrant-crime-germany-rises-50-per-cent-new-figures-show/ |archive-date=2023-06-13 |url-status=live |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2017/04/25/migrant-crime-germany-rises-50-per-cent-new-figures-show/ |last1=Huggler |first1=Justin }}</ref> The figures showed that most of the suspected crimes were by repeat offenders, and that 1 percent of migrants accounted for 40 percent of total migrant crimes.<ref name=":44" />

A 2017 study in the ''[[European Economic Review]]'' found that the German government's policy of immigration of more than 3 million people of German descent to Germany after the collapse of the Soviet Union led to a significant increase in crime.<ref name=":35" /> The effects were strongest in regions with high unemployment, high preexisting crime levels or large shares of foreigners.<ref name=":35" /> According to another 2017 study in the ''[[European Journal of Criminology]]'', the crime rate was higher among immigrant youths than native youths during the 1990s and 2000s but most of the difference could be explained by socioeconomic factors.<ref name=":50">{{Cite journal|last1=Boers|first1=Klaus|last2=Walburg|first2=Christian|last3=Kanz|first3=Kristina|date=2017|title=Crime, crime control and criminology in Germany|journal=European Journal of Criminology|volume=14|issue=6|page=654|doi=10.1177/1477370817734432|s2cid=148868401}}</ref> The different crime rates narrowed in the last ten years; the study speculates that "a new citizenship law finally granting German-born descendants of guest workers German citizenship, as well as increased integration efforts (particularly in schools) and a stronger disapproval of violence" may have contributed to this narrowing.<ref name=":50" />

In 2018, the interior ministry's report "Criminality in context with immigration" (German: ''Kriminalität im Kontext von Zuwanderung'')<ref name=":58">{{Cite web|url=https://www.bka.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/DE/Publikationen/JahresberichteUndLagebilder/KriminalitaetImKontextVonZuwanderung/KriminalitaetImKontextVonZuwanderung_2017.pdf;jsessionid=3A0357445A988BC24E4C701B5B8E6563.live2292?__blob=publicationFile&v=3|title=Kriminalität im Kontext von Zuwanderung - Bundeslagebild 2017|date=2018|website=BKA|pages=27, 55, 61|access-date=2019-09-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180802193029/https://www.bka.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/DE/Publikationen/JahresberichteUndLagebilder/KriminalitaetImKontextVonZuwanderung/KriminalitaetImKontextVonZuwanderung_2017.pdf;jsessionid=3A0357445A988BC24E4C701B5B8E6563.live2292?__blob=publicationFile&v=3|archive-date=2018-08-02}} {{verify source |date=September 2019 |reason=This ref was deleted Special:Diff/907534792 by a bug in VisualEditor and later restored by a bot from the original cite located at Special:Permalink/907533604 cite #3 - verify the cite is accurate and delete this template. [[User:GreenC bot/Job 18]]}}</ref> for the first time summarized and singled out all people who entered Germany via the asylum system. The group called "immigrants" includes all asylum seekers, tolerated people, "unauthorized residents" and all those entitled to protection (subsidiary protected, contingent refugees and refugees under the Geneva Convention and asylum). The group represented roughly 2 percent of the German population by end of 2017,<ref name="Die Welt">{{Cite news|url=https://www.welt.de/politik/deutschland/article175907770/Kriminalstatistik-Bayern-ist-das-sicherste-Bundesland.html?wtrid=onsite.onsitesearch|title=Zuwanderer in einigen Kriminalitätsfeldern besonders auffällig|date=27 April 2018|work=Die Welt|last1=Leubecher|first1=Marcel|access-date=3 September 2019|archive-date=13 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200813005832/https://www.welt.de/politik/deutschland/article175907770/Kriminalstatistik-Bayern-ist-das-sicherste-Bundesland.html?wtrid=onsite.onsitesearch|url-status=live}} {{verify source |date=September 2019 |reason=This ref was deleted Special:Diff/907534792 by a bug in VisualEditor and later restored by a bot from the original cite located at Special:Permalink/907533604 cite #4 - verify the cite is accurate and delete this template. [[User:GreenC bot/Job 18]]}}</ref> but was suspected of committing 8.5 percent of crimes (violations of the German alien law are not included). The numbers suggest that the differences could at least to some extent have to do with the fact that the refugees are younger and more often male than the average German.{{dubious|reason=https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/refugee-invaders-meme/|date=July 2019}}{{citation needed|date=July 2019}} The statistics show that the asylum-group is highly overrepresented for some types of crime. They account for 14.3 percent of all suspects in crimes against life (which include murder, manslaughter and involuntary manslaughter), 12.2 percent of sexual offences, 11.4 percent of thefts and 9.7 percent of body injuries. The report also shows differences between the origin of migrants. Syrians are underrepresented as suspects, whereas citizens from most African countries, especially northern Africans are strongly overrepresented. Migrants from Afghanistan are particularly overerrepresented as suspects in sex crimes.<ref name="Die Welt" /> In February 2019, all [[states of Germany]] reported an increase in the share of foreign and [[Statelessness|stateless]] inmates in the [[Prisons in Germany]] in the preceding 3-5 year period. In Bremen and Hamburg half the inmates were foreigners and a third in [[North Rhine-Westphalia]].<ref name=":62">{{Cite web|url=https://rp-online.de/politik/deutschland/gefaengnisse-in-deutschland-immer-mehr-auslaender-sitzen-in-haft_aid-36501705|title=Jeder Dritte in NRW: Zahl der Ausländer in Gefängnissen auf Rekordhoch|last=Mayntz|first=Gregor|website=RP ONLINE|date=4 February 2019|language=de|access-date=2019-02-22|archive-date=22 February 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190222204401/https://rp-online.de/politik/deutschland/gefaengnisse-in-deutschland-immer-mehr-auslaender-sitzen-in-haft_aid-36501705|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{bar box
| float = right
| title = Share of foreign nationals among 2017 crime suspects
|titlebar=#DDD
|caption=Source: Wall Street Journal<ref name="wsj20181016"/>
|width=250px
|bars=
{{bar percent|Pickpocketing|blue|74.4}}
{{bar percent|Forgery of official documents|blue|55.4}}
{{bar percent|Burglaries|blue|41.3}}
{{bar percent|Rapes and sexual assaults|blue|37}}
